nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light drives growth of both the forest and the coastal algae. Summer fog often cuts it along the shore.

nodes.name: Tides
nodes.desc: Rising and falling tides wet and expose the rocky shore twice a day and set where seaweeds and shellfish can live.

nodes.name: Cold Gulf of Maine water
nodes.desc: Cold, nutrient-bearing water along the coast feeds plankton and seaweed.

nodes.name: Thin glacial soils
nodes.desc: Granite bedrock and thin soils shaped by glaciers hold the forest's nutrients, which are recycled from dead matter.

nodes.name: Fungi, bacteria & detritivores
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, animals and seaweed, and return nutrients to the soil and sea.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae that grow in sunlit coastal water. They feed mussels and the tiny animals that fish eat.

nodes.name: Rockweed
nodes.desc: A brown seaweed that covers rocks in the tidal zone. Wikipedia notes that its chemical defenses deter grazing snails.

nodes.name: Balsam fir
nodes.desc: A northern conifer of the spruce-fir forest that covers most of the park's vegetated land. Deer, hares and squirrels all feed on it.

nodes.name: Red maple
nodes.desc: A common hardwood of the park's mixed forest and wetlands. Its twigs and leaves are browsed by deer and hares.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Small crustaceans that graze phytoplankton in the Gulf of Maine and are food for herring.

nodes.name: Blue mussel
nodes.desc: A filter feeder that clamps onto rocks in the tidal zone. Sea stars, whelks, gulls and eiders eat it.

nodes.name: Common periwinkle
nodes.desc: A snail that scrapes algae off intertidal rocks. Its grazing changes which seaweeds grow where.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The park's main large browser of twigs, buds and leaves. Its carcasses feed scavengers.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: Eats twigs and bark of woody plants in winter. Many predators, from foxes to eagles, depend on it.

nodes.name: American red squirrel
nodes.desc: A conifer-seed eater of the spruce-fir forest. Foxes and other predators take it.

nodes.name: Atlantic herring
nodes.desc: A schooling fish that eats copepods. It is food for seals and many seabirds.

nodes.name: Common eider
nodes.desc: A sea duck that dives for mussels and crabs along the rocky coast. Wikipedia lists mussels as a favorite food.

nodes.name: American herring gull
nodes.desc: A generalist that eats shore invertebrates such as mussels, fish, eggs and carrion. It drops shellfish on rocks to crack them.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: A small predator of hares, squirrels and voles. GloBI records it eating many park species.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: An omnivore and scavenger that feeds on carcasses and other food.

nodes.name: Harbor seal
nodes.desc: Eats mostly schooling fish such as herring. Harbor seals breed along the Maine coast.

nodes.name: Bald eagle
nodes.desc: Takes fish, ducks and gulls, and scavenges carrion. Wikipedia lists eiders and cormorants as frequent prey on the Maine coast.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: The park's top land predator. Hares and deer are among its recorded prey, and it also scavenges.
